content:
Christians and Muslims both speak of the Holy Spirit, and the same name hides two very different beliefs. For most Christians the Holy Spirit is God, the third person of the Trinity, equal to the Father and the Son. For Muslims the Holy Spirit, Ruh al-Qudus, is a created being: the angel Gabriel, who brought the revelation to the prophets.

Christian writers sometimes point to the Quran's use of the name as evidence that Muhammad (peace be upon him) borrowed it without understanding it. Muslims answer that the Quran uses it consistently and that the Hebrew Bible never makes the spirit of God a separate divine person. This article aims to provide context to both beliefs, insha'Allah, in seven answers that take both sides in turn, from the texts and from the history of the doctrine.

The Christian belief was given its classical form at the Council of Constantinople in 381, which added to the creed of Nicaea that the Holy Spirit is "the Lord and giver of life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son is worshipped and glorified." From then on, the mainstream churches have confessed the Spirit as fully God.[1]

Even after 381 the doctrine kept developing. The Western churches later added to the creed that the Spirit proceeds "from the Father and the Son," the phrase known by its Latin word, filioque.

The Eastern churches rejected the addition, and the dispute became one of the causes of the division between the Greek and Latin churches in 1054. Christians themselves did not agree on how the Spirit relates to the Father and the Son, centuries after they had agreed that the Spirit is God.[1]

The Islamic belief is stated in the Quran in a handful of verses, and the classical commentators agreed on what they mean. The Spirit is honoured, close to God and entrusted with the revelation, and it is a creature. In al-Faruqi's summary of tawhid, reality is of two kinds, Creator and creature, and "it is forever impossible that the one be united with, infused, confused with or diffused into the other."[2] On that principle no spirit sent by God can also be God.

The phrase Ruh al-Qudus, "the Spirit of holiness," occurs four times in the Quran. Three times it says that God supported Jesus with it: "We gave Jesus son of Mary the clear proofs and supported him with the Holy Spirit" (2:87; compare 2:253 and 5:110). The fourth time it names the one who brings the revelation: "Say: the Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth" (16:102).[3]

The same Spirit appears under other names. "The trustworthy Spirit (al-Ruh al-Amin) has brought it down upon your heart" (26:193-194). On the Night of Power "the angels and the Spirit descend" (97:4).

On the Day of Judgement "the Spirit and the angels stand in rows" (78:38). The Spirit is named beside the angels and ahead of them, as their chief.[3]

The Quran also calls the revelation itself a spirit: "And thus We have revealed to you a spirit of Our command" (42:52). The word ruh covers both the messenger and the message, which is why al-Tabari records that some early commentators read the Spirit that supported Jesus as the Gospel he was given.

In every use the spirit comes from God and serves His purpose: it is sent, it descends, it brings. It is never addressed in worship.[3]

The Prophet used the name in the same way. When the poet Hassan ibn Thabit answered the poets of Quraysh on his behalf, the Prophet prayed, "O God, support him with the Holy Spirit," and in another report he told him, "Answer them, and Gabriel is with you."[4]

The Quran identifies the Spirit by what he does. In 16:102 the Holy Spirit brings the revelation down. In 26:193-194 the trustworthy Spirit brings it down "upon your heart." And in 2:97: "Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel, it is he who has brought it down upon your heart by God's permission." The same act, described in the same words, is ascribed to the Holy Spirit and to Gabriel.[5]

The commentators drew the conclusion. Al-Tabari records three early opinions on "supported him with the Holy Spirit" in 2:87: that the Spirit is Gabriel, which he reports from Qatada and al-Suddi; that it is the Gospel; and that it is the name of God by which Jesus raised the dead.

He then gives his own judgement: "The most correct of these interpretations is the view of those who said that the Spirit in this place is Gabriel," because 5:110 speaks of the support as a favour given to Jesus alongside the teaching of the scripture. Ibn Kathir, three centuries later, glosses the same verse in a word: the Holy Spirit, "and he is Gabriel."[6]

The clearest picture is in Surah Maryam. "We sent to her Our Spirit, and he appeared to her as a man in full form" (19:17).

The Spirit speaks: "I am only the messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure son" (19:19). The Spirit is sent, he takes a visible form, and he calls himself a messenger of God.[7]

Luke tells the same event and names the messenger. "In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin" (Luke 1:26-27). Earlier, to Zechariah, he says of himself: "I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God, and I was sent to speak to you" (Luke 1:19).

In Luke the angel then tells Mary that "the Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you" (Luke 1:35). The Quran's account brings the two together: the Spirit sent to Mary is the messenger who stands in God's presence.[7]

The Christian doctrine claims roots in the Hebrew Bible, and the phrase "holy spirit" is there. It occurs only three times.

"Take not your Holy Spirit from me" (Psalm 51:11). "But they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit" (Isaiah 63:10, with 63:11).[8]

More often the Hebrew Bible speaks of "the spirit of God" or "the spirit of the LORD." It hovers over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2). It rushes upon Samson and gives him strength (Judges 14:6). God takes "some of the spirit that was on" Moses and puts it on seventy elders (Numbers 11:25).

In each passage the spirit is God's power or presence at work: it can be given, shared and taken away. Jewish readers have never taken these passages to describe a second or third person within God, and the Hebrew Bible never commands that the spirit be worshipped.[8]

The doctrine of the Spirit's full deity was settled late, and its own defenders said so. Gregory of Nazianzus, preaching in Constantinople in 380, the year before the council, reported the objection he faced: "From whence are you bringing in upon us this strange God, of whom Scripture is silent?" He described the views among Christians of his day: "some have conceived of him as an Activity, some as a Creature, some as God; and some have been uncertain which to call Him, out of reverence for Scripture, they say, as though it did not make the matter clear either way."[9]

Gregory's own answer is striking. "The Old Testament proclaimed the Father openly, and the Son more obscurely. The New manifested the Son, and suggested the Deity of the Spirit. Now the Spirit Himself dwells among us, and supplies us with a clearer demonstration of Himself." In his account the full doctrine of the Spirit rested on a development after the New Testament, which, he granted, only "suggested" it.[9]

This is the line al-Faruqi asks a reader to draw: between the revelation given to the prophets and what later generations built upon it. Our articles on the Trinity tested against the Hebrew Bible and on the Comma Johanneum, a later addition to 1 John that named the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit, take that history further.

One more verse is often raised. The Quran calls Jesus "a messenger of God and His word, which He conveyed to Mary, and a spirit from Him" (4:171). Does "a spirit from Him" mean that Jesus shares God's nature?

The Quran uses the same language of Adam: "When I have formed him and breathed into him of My spirit, fall down in prostration to him" (15:29; compare 32:9). It uses it of the believers: God has "supported them with a spirit from Him" (58:22). The phrase marks a gift from God and an honour, given to Adam, to Jesus and to the faithful, and the same verse, 4:171, goes on to forbid the conclusion the critic draws: "So believe in God and His messengers, and do not say Three. Desist; it is better for you. God is only one God."[10]

The bottom line

The Quran uses the name Holy Spirit consistently, for the Spirit who brings the revelation and who supported Jesus, and it identifies him with Gabriel by ascribing the same act to both. The classical commentators read it that way, and Luke names the same messenger in the story of Mary.

The Hebrew Bible speaks of God's spirit as His power and presence, never as a person to be worshipped. The full deity of the Spirit was defined in 381, after a debate whose leading defender admitted that the scriptures had only suggested it.

A Muslim can honour every verse about the Spirit and still hold, with the Quran, that the Spirit is the noblest of God's messengers and a creature of God. God knows best.

Notes

  1. The Creed of the Council of Constantinople (381), in J. N. D. Kelly, Early Christian Creeds, 3rd edition (London: Longman, 1972), chapter 10; on the filioque, Henry Chadwick, East and West: The Making of a Rift in the Church (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2003).
  2. Ismail Raji al-Faruqi, Al Tawhid: Its Implications for Thought and Life, 2nd edition (Herndon: International Institute of Islamic Thought, 1992), chapter 1.
  3. Quran 2:87; 2:253; 5:110; 16:102; 26:192–194; 97:4; 78:38; compare 70:4; 42:52.
  4. Sahih al-Bukhari 453 (Book of Prayer) and 3212 (Book of the Beginning of Creation), report of Abu Hurayra; 3213, report of al-Bara.
  5. Quran 16:102; 26:193–194; 2:97.
  6. Al-Tabari, Jami' al-Bayan, commentary on Quran 2:87 (ed. Shakir, vol. 2, pp. 320–322), reports 1485–1491 and his judgement; Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim, commentary on Quran 2:87.
  7. Quran 19:16–21; Luke 1:19, 26–35. Bible quotations follow the English Standard Version.
  8. Psalm 51:11; Isaiah 63:10–11; Genesis 1:2; Judges 14:6; Numbers 11:25.
  9. Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 31 (the Fifth Theological Oration, On the Holy Spirit), sections 1, 5 and 26, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, second series, vol. 7, translated by Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow (1894).
  10. Quran 4:171; 15:29; 32:9; 58:22.
